S1: Demographic composition and cumulative exposure percentile by cohort. (A) Proportion of the largest category of adult race (i), child race (ii), adult education (iii) and adult income (iv), by study. (B) Cumulative percent concentration of the chemical exposures assessed in the HHEAR data, by cohort. Line color gives the exposure class, each containing multiple targeted exposures; the x axis is cumulative concentration and the y axis cumulative percent. The dotted line marks the median cumulative percent for each cohort.
S2: Limit of detection across studies. (A) Distribution of the percentage of analyte measurements below the limit of detection. (B) Median percentage of results below the limit of detection, by study.
S3: Overlap of measured analytes across cohorts. (A) Analytes measured in each cohort (one row per analyte, grouped by exposure class; analyte names are listed in table S6); tiles are colored by the cohort's continent and shaded by the number of participants measured (log10 N). (B) Number of cohorts measuring each analyte, colored by whether the analyte was measured only in US cohorts, only in non-US cohorts, or in both. Of 261 analytes, 146 were measured in a single cohort and 19 in ten or more. (C) Participants contributing to each exposure class, by continent.
S4: Distribution of exposure levels across cities and locations. (A) Average exposure level by city and cohort, relative to other locations that measured the same chemical. (B) Distributional contribution of location by exposure class; the x axis is the contribution by model type and the y axis the exposure class. (C) Distributional contribution of location by exposure class in age- and sex-matched cohorts. (D) As in (C), separated into comparisons of locations within the United States, of international locations, and of US with international locations.
S5: Variation in exposure concentration within TEDDY. (A) Locations of The Environmental Determinants of Diabetes in the Young (TEDDY) study sites in Europe (Sweden, Finland and Germany) and the United States (Washington, Georgia and Colorado). (B) Distributional contribution by model type for each chemical exposure. (C) Exposure intervals for each chemical in TEDDY, by participant country; the x axis is log concentration, and the y axis and color give the location.
S6: Variation in exposure concentration within ZIP. (A) Locations of the Zika in Infants and Pregnancy (ZIP) study sites in Puerto Rico, Brazil, Guatemala and Nicaragua. (B) Distributional contribution by model type for each chemical exposure. (C) Exposure intervals for each chemical in ZIP, by participant country; the x axis is log concentration, and the y axis and color give the location.
S7: Geographic distribution of the chemical exposome under different definitions of geographic region. The x axis is log concentration and the y axis the location. Colors give the level of the geographic hierarchy: city, state, country or macroregion.
S8: Exposure sources reported by participants, within cohorts. (A) Fold difference in biomarker concentration between participants reporting a source and those not reporting it (or per doubling of a continuous source), one row per source and its main biomarker, grouped by source type; bars are 95% confidence intervals and color gives the test result (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR < 0.05; *P* < 0.05; no association; association opposite to the expected direction). The cotinine positive control is not shown. (B) The same source and biomarker pooled across cohorts by random-effects meta-analysis, with the number of cohorts and I². (C) Household drinking-water arsenic and urinary arsenic in MEBCO (Bangladesh), with the least-squares fit and its 95% confidence band; dotted lines mark the WHO (10 µg/L) and Bangladesh (50 µg/L) drinking-water limits, and water values below 0.5 µg/L are plotted at 0.5.
S9: Regional exposure data linked to HHEAR locations. (A to D) HHEAR locations over ambient PM2.5 (A), the share of households cooking with polluting fuels (B), the probability that groundwater arsenic exceeds 10 µg/L (C) and agricultural insecticide use (D); each point is a location, shaded by its median of the paired biomarker (gray, not measured). US multi-site cohorts are placed at the US interior point. (E to H) Location medians of urinary 3-PBA (E) and TCPy (F) against national insecticide use, urinary arsenic against national fish and seafood supply (G; exploratory) and urinary lead against years since the leaded-petrol ban (H). Panel annotations give Spearman ρ, permutation *P* and Benjamini-Hochberg q, computed across the pre-specified location-level tests (E, F and H) or across all location-level tests (G). Of the pre-specified tests, only 3-PBA and insecticide use remains below q = 0.05. Data sources: PM2.5 (*58*), cooking fuel (*61*), groundwater arsenic (*60*), insecticide use and fish supply (*63*) and leaded petrol (*64*).
S10: Household air and drinking water linked to HHEAR locations. (A and B) Location median 1-hydroxypyrene against population-weighted ambient PM2.5 (A) and household polluting cooking fuel (B); open points are unadjusted urine. (C) Fold change in PAH metabolites per doubling of PM2.5 in individual-level mixed models, before and after adding cooking fuel. (D) Location median urinary arsenic against groundwater arsenic; the association rests on Bangladesh. (E) US blood PFOS and PFOA against the share of public water systems in the state with the analyte detected (EPA UCMR3, 2013 to 2015). Panel annotations give Spearman ρ, permutation *P* and Benjamini-Hochberg q across all location-level tests. Data sources: PM2.5 (*58*), cooking fuel (*61*), groundwater arsenic (*60*) and drinking-water PFAS (*62*).
S11: Sample collection over time and exposures in children and mothers. (A) Distribution of sample collection years across HHEAR studies. (B) Mean log concentration of exposures measured in both children and mothers in DCHS and ELEMENT; the x axis is the log mean concentration in each group. (C) Median concentration over time by exposure class in every cohort whose sample collection spans five or more years (Fig. 2A shows six of them, selected to span four continents). Lines show yearly medians, ribbons the interquartile range and points the yearly sample size; each panel has its own log-scale axis covering the same number of decades, so slopes are comparable across cohorts but absolute levels are read from each axis. Creatinine-adjusted cohorts are in µg/g creatinine.
S12: Calendar-year trends in individual chemicals. (A) Within-cohort annual change in median concentration (% of the cohort median per sampling year; 95% confidence intervals) for every cohort in which a legacy chemical and its replacement were both measured: DEHP vs DEHTP/DINP metabolites (nuMoM2b), BPA vs BPS/BPF (TEDDY, DCHS), PFOS/PFOA vs PFNA/PFHxS (CTS, SEARCH) and the chlorpyrifos metabolite TCP vs the pyrethroid metabolite 3-PBA (DCHS). Circles, legacy chemicals; triangles, replacements; color, direction of a significant trend. All rows for these cohorts are shown, whatever the result. (B) Number of chemical × cohort pairs with a significant decrease, no significant trend, or a significant increase, by exposure class. (C) Annual change by country within TEDDY (United States, Sweden, Finland; 2012 to 2017; one protocol and laboratory) for eight chemicals; trends were largely shared across countries (year × country interaction *P* < 0.05 for 4 of 35 chemicals tested).
S13: Between-study power analysis. Estimated power to detect the between-study effect of location on exposure distributions, against model sample size, for each quantile (τ) in the child and adult cohorts.
S14: Within-study power analysis. (A) Distribution of median power across quantiles (τ) for the child and adult cohorts. (B) Distribution of estimated power within each study; the y axis is the number of models fitted and the x axis their power.
S15: Associations are contextual to the cohort from which they emerge. (A) Simulated exposure-outcome data by type of bias; the x axis is exposure (X) and the y axis outcome (Y). Thin colored lines are within-cohort fits and the heavy dark line is the naive pooled fit.
S16: Aggregate exposure in children and mothers. The x axis is the cumulative exposure score and the y axis the cohort. Each row shows the distribution, box plot and individual points for one cohort.
S17: Cumulative score and number of exposures measured. (A) Cumulative score against the number of exposures measured in the child cohorts, colored by cohort. (B) As in (A), for the adult cohorts.
S18: Quantile-quantile plots of the cumulative exposure score. Each panel shows the normal quantile-quantile plot of the cumulative score for one cohort; the x axis is the theoretical quantile and the y axis the sample quantile.
S19: Correlation between exposome variables and the exposure score. (A) Absolute within-class correlation coefficients for all measured exposures in the pooled HHEAR cohort, in adults and children. (B) Effective number of features (Meff), original number of features (M) and their difference, by exposure class. (C) Aggregate exposure score against the percentage of an individual's exposures in the top tertile across all studies. (D) Distributional contribution of each sociodemographic model fitted within each HHEAR cohort; the x axis is the contribution by model type and the y axis the study. (E) Within-cohort sociodemographic contribution for individual chemicals in every cohort (averaged across the cohort's chemicals), by model term (sampling year, age, sex, education, race and ethnicity, and other sociodemographic variables, as available in each cohort); the x axis is the contribution to prediction (mean R²) and the y axis the study.
S20: Sample matrix is confounded with geography and inflates the estimated contribution of location. (A) Median concentration of each trace element measured in both blood and urine across HHEAR cohorts, on a log scale; lines join the blood and urine medians. Analytes shown are those assayed in both media, which reflects data availability rather than representative sampling of the panel. (B) Distributional contribution of location by exposure class, from the model in which blood and urine cohorts are pooled (grey) and from models restricted to urine (blue) or blood (gold) cohorts. Classes measured in one matrix only fall on the pooled value and serve as an internal control. Both panels use the same censored quantile-regression procedure; only the set of rows entering the model differs.
S21: Population structure changes inference: serum PFAS. (A) Percentage of participants above the pooled HHEAR 90th percentile for PFOA and PFOS, by cohort (median sampling year) and population panel. The dashed line marks 10%, the share each cohort would have flagged under its own (population-specific) 90th percentile. Across all eligible serum PFAS comparisons, agreement between pooled and population-specific classification was moderate (median Cohen's κ = 0.53) and the pooled reference missed 42% of participants who were highly exposed relative to their own population. (B) Child LDL cholesterol against PFOS (log(1 + ng/mL)) in GOALS, NASH and SEARCH: each cohort's own linear fit, cohort means (circles) with 95% confidence intervals for mean LDL (vertical) and mean PFOS (horizontal), the n-weighted trend across cohort means, and the naive pooled fit; y-axis restricted to the central 90% of LDL values; the vertical band at the left is NASH children with PFOS below the limit of detection. (C) Slope estimates with 95% confidence intervals: each cohort, the cohort-adjusted estimate (study fixed effects; equal to the within-cohort term, Bw, of a within-between decomposition) and the naive pooled estimate. Unadjusted linear models.
S22: Exposure-outcome associations under different treatments of cohort. Standardized associations for the 44 maternal exposure-outcome pairs in Fig. 3B, unadjusted and in the same order as that panel. (A) Cohort fixed-effects estimates with 95% confidence intervals, equal to the within-cohort term (Bw) of a within-between decomposition; naive pooled estimates that ignore cohort; and random-effects meta-analysis of within-cohort estimates. (B) Between-cohort term (Bb) of the same decomposition. As in Fig. 3B, naive estimates are scaled by total standard deviations and within-cohort estimates by within-cohort standard deviations; meta-analysis and Bb use the within-cohort scale. Values beyond an axis limit are drawn at the limit. Numbers in parentheses give the number of cohorts where there are more than two.
